paras: The driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia, took place in late 1881, when striking coal miners in Fayette County turned back the first group of Black miners that operators had brought from Virginia to replace them. Troops were then called to guard a second group, and the Wheeling Register printed two conflicting accounts of how serious the confrontation had been.

About 500 men at the soft-coal mines of Coal Valley, in the Kanawha mining region, struck for an advance of fifteen cents a ton. The operators said they could not pay it unless the Chesapeake and Ohio railroad paid more for coal, and they then imported "colored miners" from Virginia.

According to Fayette prosecutor J. W. St. Clair, the strikers got the first imported group to quit "by threatening their lives," while miners' wives gathered at the pitmouth with pans and sticks and several hundred men stood nearby. He said some of the new hands crawled out through the mine's air-course rather than face "the mob."

When a second group of Black miners arrived, about 400 strikers waited for them at the station. Sheriff Tyree obtained the Governor's permission to call out troops, and two companies guarded the new hands for a couple of days until the strikers dispersed.

No arrests are reported in the coverage, and St. Clair said trespassers could not be punished under existing law and witnesses would not testify against the miners' union. He said he had advised operators that they could arm employees and "shoot and drag" strikers off posted property.

Both accounts appeared in the Wheeling Register. On 3 December its correspondent, sent to check "Alarming Reports" of lawlessness, wrote that the first batch had been "dissuaded," the peace never broken, and the troop call "a serious mistake." On 14 December it printed St. Clair's version under the subheading "Force With Force" without comment.

The two accounts differ on whether the strikers threatened the Black miners' lives: the correspondent said they stopped "short of violence," while the prosecutor, who backed calling the troops, described death threats and a mob.

reader.title: Driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia
bases: Striking miners in a wage dispute drove imported Black replacement miners from a mine and gathered to stop a second group, which troops then guarded (A2, A3).

Two separately sourced Wheeling Register reports, a correspondent's visit (A2) and the Fayette prosecutor's interview (A3), agree that strikers turned back the first batch of imported Black miners and that troops were called, though they differ on whether lives were threatened.

accounts.label: Wheeling Register correspondent
accounts.gist: The strikers did all they could 'short of violence' to dissuade others; the first batch of Virginia negroes was dissuaded from work, the peace was never broken, and calling troops was premature, as officers themselves admitted.

accounts.label: Fayette prosecutor J. W. St. Clair
accounts.gist: The old hands stopped the first imported negroes by threatening their lives, women massed at the pitmouth with pans and sticks backed by several hundred men, and some new hands crawled out through the air-course; 400 strikers then met the next lot until two companies of troops guarded them.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Register first framed the affair as overblown 'Alarming Reports' and a wage dispute caused by the C. & O. railroad (A2), then printed the prosecutor's 'Force With Force' account of a 'mob' and threats without comment (A3); neither report gives the Black miners' own version.

versions.value: Strikers 'dissuaded' the first batch, 'short of violence'; peace not broken; no trouble beyond civil authorities' control
Strikers threatened the new hands' lives; a demonstration by women and several hundred men scared them out, some escaping through the air-course

conflicts.note: A2 is a correspondent's on-the-scene summary that says officers admitted troops were not needed; A3 is the account of the prosecutor who supported calling troops, an interested official.
